segments.text: Sonae. The agent team that stands watch over your family. Built for the AWS Agents for Humans hackathon, on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Japan asks every household to prepare a personal evacuation timeline: who does what, at which official alert level. That means reading two hundred page hazard maps, learning which evacuation site covers which disaster, and negotiating it all with your family. It is homework assigned to a hundred and twenty five million people. Almost no one has done it.

And the people with the least capacity to do it need it most. About eighty percent of Japan's flood fatalities are people over sixty five. Often an aging parent, alone in the family home, hours away from their children.

The night of Typhoon Hagibis, twenty nineteen. The Chikuma river reached flood warning footing at five thirty in the afternoon, in daylight. The evacuation order came at eleven forty at night, in darkness and driving rain. Before dawn the levee failed, and the district flooded to the rooftops. The information was public the whole time. What families lacked was an agent on watch.

This is Sonae. Give it one address, and a few sentences about your family. A Cartographer agent reads the statutory hazard maps at that exact coordinate. A Planner drafts the family's timeline, tuned to a grandmother's knees. And before anything reaches you, an adversarial Verifier re-derives every claim from the same official data. You review the plan, and approve it. Once, calmly. From here, Sonae is authorized to act.
Now, October eleventh, twenty nineteen, replayed minute by minute from the official record. The day before landfall: level one. Charge the phone. Pack the medication. While the sky is clear.
Saturday afternoon, the river reaches advisory levels. Level two. Valuables upstairs, walking shoes by the door.

Three thirty PM. An emergency heavy rain warning, the first in Nagano's history. Formally, that is level five equivalent. But Sonae's Sentinel knows what it means operationally: the roads are still dry, and this is the last, best window to leave. It activates level four. Complete the evacuation now. And watch the verifier: it rejected the first draft for over-claiming an evacuation order that did not exist yet, then approved the corrected message. Verified, cited, in each person's own language. It is still daylight.

Then, discipline. Landslide advisories for other districts. River bulletins the plan already covers. The Sentinel stands by through all of them. A family that trusts its agent is a family that acts when it speaks.
Eight fifty PM. The river starts coming over its banks upstream. Level five. Final confirmation that everyone is out, and that nobody goes back in. Safety check-ins open on every phone.

Eleven forty PM. The official evacuation order, when the real residents of Hoyasu were told to leave. And at one fifteen, the river came over the levee at their doorstep. Sonae's journal simply reads: stand by. The family had been safe for eight hours.

After the water, Japanese neighborhoods confirm safety with paper name lists, carried door to door. Sonae's circle mode replaces the paper, not the neighbors. Live check-ins across households, and a Coordinator agent that tells the chairman exactly which door to knock on first: the eighty eight year old, still unconfirmed.

None of this is a demo trick. These are real catches from our flight recorder. AI prose fails closed: unverified text is never sent. The official signal fails open: relayed verbatim rather than silenced. And the family's approval is the authorization boundary.

Under the hood, a self-correcting Strands graph builds the plan, and a verified pipeline runs the watch, with typed JSON between agents and flight recorder hooks on every tool call. It runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: deployed, stateful in S3, with an EventBridge heartbeat. We verified the whole chain in the cloud, including the planning graph converging inside the runtime. On a calm day, a watch cycle costs zero model tokens. Boring is the job.

Everything you saw runs on public government data. Hazard maps, shelter registries, live weather feeds. Built for Japan, and portable to any country that publishes its hazards. Sonae. Because the next Hagibis is already forming, and every family deserves someone on watch.
